thread.title: When Life Gives You Lemons, Beat The S&P 500 Index

author: Dale Roberts
title: When Life Gives You Lemons, Beat The S&P 500 Index
text:
Seeking Alpha author Ploutos offered this wonderful article, Even The Fallen Dividend Aristocrats Outperformed the Market .
In that post, Ploutos showed how staying true to Dividend Aristocrats ( NOBL ) through thick and thin would have allowed investors to beat the market ( IVV ) over longer periods.
As we know, the last major market correction was known as the Financial Crisis. The epicenter of the market collapse was the US banks and other financials. We can see that those 10 US banks that were removed from the Dividend Achievers Index due to a dividend cut or freeze underperformed the market over 5- and 10-year periods, but outperformed if we look at trailing 20-year performance. Keep in mind this article was posted in February of 2016.
Those banks had built up enough of a lead over the market from 1997 and into 2016 that the lead held up through the recession and beyond. That said, the 10 financial companies were certainly whacked in the recession and fell by over 70%. The 10 fallen financials are Bank of America ( BAC ), BB&T Corporation ( BBT ), Comerica Inc. ( CMA ), First Horizon National ( FHN ), KeyCorp ( KEY ), M&T Bank Corporation ( MTB ), Regions Financial Corporation ( RF ), Synovus Financial ( SNV ), State Street Corporation ( STT ) and U.S. Bancorp ( USB ).
Here are the financials vs. IVV from January of 2007 through to end of 2017. The chart is courtesy of portfoliovisualizer.com.
Not very pretty. Of course, these are time weighted returns starting with $100,000 with dividend reinvestment. It's a static amount with no regular contribution. In the accumulation stage, most investors will add monies on a regular schedule. That's an investment staple wealth-building practice.
What if an investor stuck by their disbanded Aristocrats and continued to invest on a regular schedule? Here's a scenario where the investor invests $1,000 monthly on a regular schedule from 2007 through to end of 2017. The contributions are increased for inflation. And typically, as we make more monies, we will usually increase our investment contributions. That will happen automatically for anyone who has a work group plan where contributions and company matched contributions are based on salary.
Here's the 10 fallen financials vs. IVV. Portfolio 1 is the 10 financials. January of 2017 is a terrible start date for the financials as they had already begun their market correction, the financials led the way in that regard. Sometimes the market makers know what's going on. But was it wise to abandon them, as did the active managers?
We see that by end of 2017, the market losers had turned into winners. The fallen financials beat the S&P 500 index fund IVV with new contributions and a reinvestment plan. Chalk up another one or three for an investor's greatest weapons. Full disclosure, the financials fell again in 2018. That can happen when we have that concentration risk.
Time + Consistency + Patience
The above strategy would mean the investor would have to ignore just about everything and everyone. That investor perhaps did a little bit of 'value hunting'. The portfolio is rebalanced on an annual schedule. That increases the value hunting, taking any gains from the outperformers and moving the funds to the underperformers.
We see that the regular investment schedule turned a miserable time weighted TWRR return of 3.3% CAGR into a very impressive money weighted (personal) return of 13.82%. Buy low as they say.
Consistency and patience can be the great equalizer with respect to total returns.
Another lesson from the returns chart is that when an investor is starting out and is investing on a regular schedule, the new monies can mitigate or eliminate the price risk. Advisors might often suggest that new investors (who don't yet know their risk tolerance level) might start quite conservatively as they could 'lose' 50% in a major correction. But if risk is the fear of getting scared due to having to watch a portfolio decline in value; those new monies might mean that the investor might not have to watch the portfolio decline at all. Also, risk is related to how much you have invested. It's easier to watch $3,000 of value disappear compared to watching a portfolio decline of $300,000. Things look and feel different when we are beginning our investment journey.
New investors should consider how their portfolio with an automatic investment plan will react in the early stages; they might consider what the personal returns chart might look like as well, even through a major correction. Things might not look that bad. A new investor might be able to take on an aggressive portfolio in the early stages if they understand the above chart and scenario.
And on consistency and time and sticking with those losers, the 10 fallen financials would have beat the Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF ( VIG ) from 2007 to end of 2017. The Achievers Index applies financial filters that attempts to remove the trouble makers, ahead of time. It was able to find and remove many of the financials, but not all. But we see there was perhaps no value in that exercise with respect to total returns for the 'dollar cost averager'.
My readers will know that I sold my VIG and skimmed 15 Dividend Achievers in 2015. I have ignored the index that has removed a few of the names as per those dividend health screens. It appears to have been a good strategy to ignore those smart beta filters. Here's my article, Looks Like Smart Beta Just Got Dumb and Dumber .
So much for 'active' management. There's just so much evidence that investors simply need to buy enough very good companies; and from there stay the course, ignore the noise/experts, and invest on a regular schedule.
Buy. Hold. Add.
Here's my no-look 15 Achievers vs. VIG from January of 2015 to end of November 2018. The 15 Dividend Achievers is Portfolio 1.
It's more than surprising that some investment experts simply don't give the dividend the respect that it deserves. The most well-known Canadian ETF and index model portfolio site Canadian Couch Potato will often suggest that there is no benefit to dividends or dividend growth. We know that the meaningful dividend growth history can work as a divining rod that can potentially find durable profitability and greater long-term financial health. While the 10 fallen financials were hit hard, none of the companies disappeared. As a group, they were a decent investment with a regular reinvestment schedule. Sometimes, we have to give our losers some love.
I'll continue to offer dividend options on my site and on the ETF Model Portfolio page. Just as I'll suggest investors use the size premium to potentially boost returns beyond the broad market indices.
But once again, the most important 'lesson' from this post might be that patience and consistency is a powerful weapon when combined with a longer time horizon.
